tagline: Rolling hills, farmland and waterfalls along two Pennsylvania state routes
intro: The Laurel Highlands Scenic Byway follows 68 miles of Routes 711 and 381 through rolling hills, farmland and woodland. VisitPA highlights waterfalls and Frank Lloyd Wright buildings along the drive. On its southern section, Route 381 curves through forests and fields, crosses the Youghiogheny River at Ohiopyle and passes through tracts of Forbes State Forest near the West Virginia line. The Laurel Highlands byway designation took effect on September 11, 1996, joining portions of PA 711 and PA 381 into a corridor from the Conemaugh River to West Virginia.

The numbered highway came before the scenic designation: PA 711 was first signed in 1928, with construction continuing into the early 1930s. In the 1950s, its southern endpoint moved from Pleasant Grove to Belle Vernon; another move in the 1960s established the current endpoint at Connellsville. The Ohiopyle crossing is a two-lane highway bridge opened in 1975, the third bridge in that vicinity, following a nineteenth-century covered bridge and a later Pratt truss.

Driving south from Seward, follow PA 711 through Ligonier and Stahlstown to Donegal. The byway continues through Jones Mills to Normalville, where PA 381 carries it south. Beyond Mill Run, Fallingwater lies west of the road; then come Ohiopyle, Farmington and the final wooded stretch to the state line.

moments.title: Fort Ligonier
moments.text: Fort Ligonier began as the last fortified link on General John Forbes’s new road across Pennsylvania toward French-held Fort Duquesne. Built in 1758, it served as a staging area for that campaign and later as a passage post to Fort Pitt. The garrison was decommissioned in 1766. What occupies the original site now is a reconstruction, opened in 1953 after archaeological work began in 1947. Wooden defenses, a moat and a storehouse give physical form to the post; the adjacent museum includes exhibits on the excavations that helped recover its layout.

moments.title: Fallingwater
moments.text: Fallingwater places part of a three-story country house directly over Bear Run’s waterfall. Frank Lloyd Wright designed it as a weekend retreat for Pittsburgh department-store owner Edgar J. Kaufmann Sr. and his wife Liliane. The family began using the house in 1937; the guest wing followed in 1939. Its terraces extend from the chimney without supports at their outer ends. The terraces sagged, and major repairs in the late 1990s and early 2000s addressed structural defects and poor drainage. Local stone, reinforced concrete, steel and glass make up the house.
moments.notice: Notice the terraces extending outward from the chimney, unsupported at their outer ends.

moments.title: Ohiopyle
moments.text: At Ohiopyle, a 20-foot waterfall spans the Youghiogheny River. Railroads once brought visitors from Pittsburgh to see the falls and stay in riverside resorts, where the attractions included dancing pavilions and bowling alleys. As automobile travel displaced that resort trade, the buildings were demolished and forest regrew. The Western Pennsylvania Conservancy bought the land and sold it to the Commonwealth. Ohiopyle State Park opened in 1965, with formal dedication following in 1971. The falls now occupy the center of the park’s Falls Day Use Area. The borough itself is surrounded by the state park.
